article_title: Green Dot Public Schools
citation: Green Dot Public Schools. (2018). WWC Intervention Report: Green Dot Public Schools, Charter Schools. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.greendot.org
title: Large high school divided into multiple small charter schools as a turnaround design
description: This whole-school design pattern converts one existing, underperforming public high school into a set of smaller autonomous charter schools sharing the same neighborhood catchment. The reviewed study "examined a group of Green Dot Public Schools formed by dividing an existing public high school into a set of smaller schools": the original school was divided into two off-site small schools in the first year and into eight schools by the second year, serving the full prior student community. The pattern pairs small-school community with the charter operator's six-principle model.
requirements: Chartering and district authorization to convert an existing district-run school
Funding for transformation operations, which in the reported case came largely from private foundations
constraints: Evidence for the pattern comes from one quasi-experimental study meeting WWC standards with reservations in a single urban district
target_learners: Ninth-through-twelfth-grade students in an underperforming urban high school catchment
target_learning_goals: Improved achievement, attendance, and graduation in a turnaround setting
examples: Green Dot started converting the LAUSD school with two off-site small schools in 2007–08 and reached eight schools by fall 2008, spending approximately $15 million over a 4-year turnaround

article_title: Learning Analytics Dashboard Design and Evaluation to Support Student Self-Regulation of Study Behaviour
citation: de Vreugd, L., van Leeuwen, A., Jansen, R., & van der Schaaf, M. (2024). Learning Analytics Dashboard Design and Evaluation to Support Student Self-Regulation of Study Behaviour. Journal of Learning Analytics, 11(3), 249–262. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2024.8529
title: Do not rely solely on stakeholder input for LAD content; provide literature-based constructs for stakeholders to weigh
description: This principle holds that needs assessment for a learning analytics dashboard should combine stakeholder preferences with constructs drawn from literature. The article recommends that "developers do not solely rely on stakeholder input" because users may be unaware of LAD possibilities; presenting potentially relevant constructs from literature lets stakeholders weigh their added value against their own ideas, resulting in better-informed preferences. In this study, focus groups rated a predetermined literature-based list and could add new topics.
requirements: Stakeholders such as students and tutors must be given a predetermined list of potentially relevant constructs from literature alongside the option to suggest new topics
constraints: Relying solely on prospective user preferences is advised against, as users may not be aware of LAD possibilities or mechanisms of data collection
target_learners: University students
examples: Focus group participants rated predetermined constructs (e.g., self-efficacy, intrinsic goal orientation) on Likert scales and could add new topics; two newly suggested topics per group made the final ranking lists.
key_sources: de Vreugd, L., van Leeuwen, A., Jansen, R., & van der Schaaf, M. (2024). Learning Analytics Dashboard Design and Evaluation to Support Student Self-Regulation of Study Behaviour. Journal of Learning Analytics, 11(3), 249–262. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2024.8529

article_title: Learning Analytics Dashboard Design and Evaluation to Support Student Self-Regulation of Study Behaviour
citation: de Vreugd, L., van Leeuwen, A., Jansen, R., & van der Schaaf, M. (2024). Learning Analytics Dashboard Design and Evaluation to Support Student Self-Regulation of Study Behaviour. Journal of Learning Analytics, 11(3), 249–262. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2024.8529
title: Plan an explicit usability exploration and adjustment phase before evaluating a LAD's perceived usefulness
description: The article recommends that LAD developers "plan an explicit phase of usability exploration and design adjustments before evaluating a LAD's usefulness." Think-aloud protocols provided in-depth insight into usability problems and, most importantly, the reasons for them, allowing design adjustments (e.g., an introduction video, reorganized exercises) before the usefulness evaluation. Needs assessment, usability testing, and perceived usefulness evaluation are described as all essential elements of a LAD's final evaluation of effectiveness.
requirements: Think-aloud interviews or comparable qualitative exploration to identify why usability problems occur, followed by design adjustments before usefulness assessment
target_learners: University students
examples: Think-aloud interviews (n=8) revealed participants struggled with navigating an empty LAD and interpreting acceptable scores; adjustments such as an introduction video and Prepare–Act–Reflect categorization preceded the SUS reassessment.

article_title: The Forgotten Year
citation: Seeskin, A., Mahaffie, S., & Usher, A. (2020). The forgotten year: Applying lessons from Freshman success to Sophomore year. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/the-forgotten-year-applying-lessons-freshman-success-sophomore-year
title: Sophomore educators should use a layered indicator system combining on-track status, course failures, attendance, and a 3.0 GPA threshold to target supports
description: The report recommends that sophomore educators combine multiple predictive indicators rather than relying on on-track status alone. "By using an indicator system that combines all of these key predictive indicators—a GPA threshold of 3.0, in addition to the three warning indicators for high school graduation—sophomore educators could differentiate their students" and target supports effectively. The GPA threshold matters because GPA is the strongest indicator of college access, while failures and attendance best flag non-graduation risk.
requirements: Access to timely, actionable data on grades, attendance, and course failures for each student
constraints: Indicators alone cannot change a system; they must be paired with monitoring structures and supports such as freshman success teams extended to sophomore year
target_learners: High school sophomores, including students off-track or showing early warning signs
examples: CPS freshman teams already use eighth-grade attendance and grades at entry, then monitor Freshman OnTrack status and GPA throughout the year; the report proposes extending this structure to sophomore year.
key_sources: Seeskin, A., Mahaffie, S., & Usher, A. (2020). The forgotten year: Applying lessons from Freshman success to Sophomore year. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/the-forgotten-year

article_title: Recruitment and Retention: Impact of Pilot Solutions Designed by Teachers of Color Phase II Report
citation: Iloh, C. (2024, February). Recruitment and Retention: Impact of Pilot Solutions Designed by Teachers of Color (Phase II). Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/216
title: Latino/a Affinity Group at Huntley 158: an affinity space fostering belonging and retention of Latino/a teachers
description: Huntley Community School District 158 initiated a Latino/a Affinity Group "to foster connections and support among Latino/a teachers, creating a sense of belonging and networking opportunities across the district to improve staff retention." Emerging from a Digital Promise-facilitated design studio, it gave educators a platform for personal and professional growth, enabled cross-school collaboration on teaching practices, and supported student-facing events such as a fourth-grade dance performance that centered Latino/a identity.
requirements: Time and space for members across school locations to meet and compare practices
constraints: Focused on Latino/a staff in a district with fast-growing Latino/a enrollment that faculty demographics do not match
target_learners: Latino/a teachers and staff
target_learning_goals: Retention, job satisfaction, belonging, collaborative professional growth
examples: A teacher reported feeling "like a leader" and exchanging practices with language and monolingual colleagues

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning
citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., Blitz, J., & Garcia-Arena, P. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Language development time should connect to grade-level content and disciplinary practices, not isolated grammar or vocabulary drills
description: The brief argues that not all opportunities to use language are equivalent and that lessons are most effective when they engage students in thinking about how specific language achieves a communicative purpose. It warns that "Time spent concentrating on grammatical, lexical, or morphological structures for their own sake should be avoided," giving as counterexamples vocabulary lists, verb conjugation, or translation disconnected from content under study.
requirements: Targeted language development must reflect and connect to current grade-level content learning and disciplinary practices
target_learners: English learners in content-area instruction
target_learning_goals: Linguistic skills and knowledge required to operate independently in content-area classrooms
examples: In math, teachers design activities drawing attention to specialized meanings for common terms like unit or rate in word problems; in science, teachers provide model sentences with linking words such as 'Plants need roots because they bring in nutrients.'

article_title: Community Schools in Los Angeles Unified: Transforming Teaching and Learning
citation: Klevan, S., Spitzer, N., Hernández, L., Rubinstein, C., & Swain, W. (2026). Community schools in Los Angeles Unified: Transforming teaching and learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/677.130
title: LAUSD community school common roles and processes (coordinator, community rep, assets and needs assessment, benchmarks)
description: Each LAUSD community school implements common roles, processes, and structures codified in the collective bargaining agreement. The report states: "These common positions—codified and outlined in the CBA between the district and the union—include the community school coordinator (CSC) and the community representative (community rep)." The CSC builds community partnerships, family engagement, and leads the assets and needs assessment (ANA), a comprehensive stakeholder-data process revisited annually; community reps support day-to-day implementation and home–school relationship building. Schools also use phased benchmarks (short-, medium-, and long-term outcomes) as a roadmap for transformation, and inclusive school-based decision-making bodies composed of community members, staff, families, and students.
requirements: Annual district funding for a community school coordinator and community representative at each school site
An assets and needs assessment conducted in the first year and revised in subsequent years
constraints: Roles remain flexible and vary depending on the needs of each specific school site
target_learners: Students and families in LAUSD community schools
target_learning_goals: School transformation, family engagement, and continuous improvement grounded in community needs
examples: The Business and Tourism CSC described surveying students and staff, disseminating findings, and creating data-grounded school priorities
key_sources: Klevan, S., Spitzer, N., Hernández, L., Rubinstein, C., & Swain, W. (2026). Community schools in Los Angeles Unified: Transforming teaching and learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/677.130

article_title: AI-based scoring systematically underestimates conceptual understanding of linguistically weak students' explanations in physics
citation: Markus S. Feser & Paul L. Tschisgale. (2026). AI-based scoring systematically underestimates conceptual understanding of linguistically weak students' explanations in physics. Physics Education, Leibniz Institute for Science and Mathematics Education, Kiel. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8503-0951
title: Language bias in assessing text-based explanations as a task-inherent challenge of inferring conceptual understanding through language
description: The article proposes that language bias — the systematic influence of lexical and syntactic quality on assessments of conceptual understanding — is not merely a flaw of particular assessors. Because explanations "are linguistic representations through which that understanding is communicated", any assessor must identify evidence of understanding within linguistic features, and imprecise vocabulary and syntax can obscure that evidence. The finding that AI-based scoring reproduces the bias previously documented for STEM teachers supports framing the problem as inherent to the scoring task itself, spanning human and AI assessment in STEM education.
requirements: Assessment of conceptual understanding must rely on text-based explanations from which understanding can only be inferred indirectly
constraints: The article's evidence comes from German-language physics explanations of a single task by secondary-school students; generalization to other STEM fields, languages, and formats requires further research
target_learners: secondary-school physics students
multilingual and international learners
examples: The study compared eleven AI-based scoring approaches against independently assigned expert scores for conceptual understanding and linguistic quality on the spacewalk task
key_sources: Markus S. Feser & Paul L. Tschisgale. (2026). AI-based scoring systematically underestimates conceptual understanding of linguistically weak students' explanations in physics. article_title: Do Assessment Instruments Measure the Same Thing for Humans and LLMs? A Latent Structure Analysis
citation: Alona Strugatski, Licol Zeinfeld, Giora Alexandron. (2026). Do Assessment Instruments Measure the Same Thing for Humans and LLMs? A Latent Structure Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15630
title: A validity-oriented framework for comparing assessment latent structure across humans and LLMs
description: The article introduces a methodological framework that treats similarity of latent factor structure as a necessary, though not sufficient, condition for transferring score interpretations from humans to LLMs. It combines exploratory factor analysis, factor congruence with Hungarian-algorithm factor matching, and repeated resampling against a human-human baseline. As the authors state, it "introduces a validity-oriented framework for comparing the latent structure of assessments across humans and LLMs", demonstrated through two case studies showing instruments "may capture substantially different constructs in humans and LLMs".
requirements: Requires human and LLM response data on the same item set, with preprocessing (removing zero-variance items and unstable tetrachoric correlation estimates) before factor retention and extraction.
Requires a human-human resampling baseline, since within-human similarity is itself variable across resamples.
constraints: The article states it addresses only one aspect of validity, internal structure; generalization to related tasks measuring the same abilities is not examined.
target_learners: Grade 11-12 chemistry students
university entrance exam examinees
LLM systems evaluated on educational assessments
target_learning_goals: validity of LLM capability claims from educational assessments
examples: Applied to a 22-item chemistry diagnostic (931 students) and a 20-item quantitative reasoning section (over 4,800 examinees), with responses from six multimodal LLMs pooled into one group of 120 response sets per instrument.
key_sources: Alona Strugatski, Licol Zeinfeld, Giora Alexandron. (2026). Do Assessment Instruments Measure the Same Thing for Humans and LLMs? A Latent Structure Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15630

article_title: Once a Response, Always a Response: Detecting LLM-generated Text via Latent Prompt Restoration
citation: Hongrui Bao, Yubing Ren, Jinhan You, Fang Fang, Shi Wang, Yanan Cao. (2026). ONCE A RESPONSE, ALWAYS A RESPONSE: DETECTING LLM-GENERATED TEXT VIA LATENT PROMPT RESTORATION. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05741
title: Latent prompt dependency: machine-generated text retains a detectable assistant-response context after the original prompt is removed
description: The article proposes that instruction-tuned LLMs produce text conditioned on prompts, and that although the original prompt is removed, its influence persists: the text still implicitly remembers it was a response. EchoPrompt operationalizes this by restoring a generic assistant-response context and measuring context-conditioned likelihood gain. The authors state the hidden dependency "can be partially reactivated by prepending a unified generic prefix", making it a discriminative signal between machine and human text.
requirements: Detection requires paired base and instruction-tuned proxy models and a fixed generic assistant-style prefix
constraints: The signal is weaker for non-chat/completion outputs from models that do not rely on instruction-tuned assistant behavior
target_learners: researchers and platform moderators detecting LLM-generated text
examples: EchoPrompt prepends the fixed prefix 'You are a helpful, versatile, and intelligent AI assistant...' to each evaluated passage before dual-model scoring
key_sources: Hongrui Bao, Yubing Ren, Jinhan You, Fang Fang, Shi Wang, Yanan Cao. (2026). ONCE A RESPONSE, ALWAYS A RESPONSE: DETECTING LLM-GENERATED TEXT VIA LATENT PROMPT RESTORATION. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05741

article_title: Layer-Sensitive Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Assisted Writing: Supported Performance and Independent No-AI Outcomes
citation: Chen X (2026) Layer-sensitive cognitive offloading in generative AI-assisted writing: supported performance and independent no-AI outcomes. Front. Psychol. 17:1906199. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906199
title: Layer-sensitive account of cognitive offloading in GenAI-assisted writing
description: The article proposes a four-layer account of cognitive offloading in GenAI-assisted writing, distinguishing surface, structural, idea, and reasoning offloading as "related but non-equivalent dimensions". Surface offloading concerns grammar, vocabulary, and local expression; structural offloading concerns outlines, sequencing, and global organization; idea offloading concerns claims, examples, and content directions; reasoning offloading concerns warrants, counterarguments, evidence interpretation, and argumentative logic. The framework treats frequency of AI use as insufficient, since one reasoning-generation request may matter more than several language requests.
requirements: Primary layer scores derived from coded interaction and revision evidence, with brief self-report used only for triangulation
constraints: The article states the offloading framework showed promising initial structural, reliability, and convergence evidence but requires independent validation
target_learners: Chinese L1 undergraduates writing academic English
examples: Layer scores were coded from prompts, AI outputs, adoption decisions, and draft–revision records; a four-factor model fit substantially better than a one-factor model (CFI = 0.959 vs 0.585)
key_sources: Chen X (2026) Layer-sensitive cognitive offloading in generative AI-assisted writing: supported performance and independent no-AI outcomes. Front. Psychol. 17:1906199. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906199

article_title: Policy Fragmentation or Institutional Alignment? Institutional Governance of AI in Universities and Business Schools
citation: Lydia Manikonda and Dominique Outlaw. (2026). Policy Fragmentation or Institutional Alignment? Institutional Governance of AI in Universities and Business Schools.
title: Layer AI governance: a university-wide risk-management base with unit-specific contextual policies
description: The article proposes that institutions govern AI in two coordinated layers: a foundational university-wide policy ensuring "consistency, legal compliance, and academic integrity across all disciplines", and unit-specific contextual policies that honor university guidelines while fostering student learning. It further recommends integrating procurement needs with teaching needs, standardizing disclosure across courses, and maintaining a continuous feedback loop between pedagogy and policy with regular review as technology and workforce demands evolve.
requirements: University-wide guardrails addressing transparency, plagiarism definitions, and strict rules prohibiting upload of sensitive information to AI platforms
Collaborative mechanisms such as inter-department policy committees comprising faculty across units and students across disciplines
constraints: The goal is not a one-size-fits-all solution but a framework institutions adapt to their specific contexts
target_learners: higher education students, particularly business and finance students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking to evaluate AI-generated outputs
examples: The article recommends starting with the University-wide risk management policy, then adding department-level contextual policies that mitigate confusion while honoring university-wide guidelines.
key_sources: Lydia Manikonda and Dominique Outlaw. (2026). Policy Fragmentation or Institutional Alignment? Institutional Governance of AI in Universities and Business Schools. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03584

article_title: Ontology-Based Layered Hybrid AI-Driven Knowledge Model for Personalized E-Learning
citation: Tatyana Ivanova. (2026). Ontology-Based Layered Hybrid AI-Driven Knowledge Model for Personalized E-Learning. Mathematics 2026, 14, 808. https://doi.org/10.3390/math14050808
title: Layered tutoring domain ontology system from upper-level to task-oriented sub-domain ontologies
description: The article organizes tutoring domain knowledge as a layered system of ontologies: an upper-level domain ontology for very general concepts and alignment, cross-domain ontologies for interoperability across related subjects, core domain ontologies for generic subject concepts, educational domain ontologies for single tutoring subjects (coarse-grained for curriculum planning and fine-grained for performance-based personalized learning), and task-oriented sub-domain ontologies such as assessment-linked, competency-based, prerequisite, and problem-solving ontologies. The article states that layered systems let "complex knowledge can be represented in a well-structured, modular, and evolvable way, separating general from specific entities."
requirements: Layered models must define roles and responsibilities of layers, ensuring interchangeability or evolution of specific ontology implementations
constraints: The number of layers and ontologies in every layer depends on the specific implementation
target_learners: learners in IESs and ITSs using adaptive personalized learning and tutoring
target_learning_goals: semantic search, navigation, personalized tutoring, resource recommendation, learning content reuse and interoperability
examples: Examples printed include the school geometry ontology, core computer science ontology, ACM computing classification, and assessment-linked ontologies for automatic quiz generation
key_sources: Tatyana Ivanova. (2026). Ontology-Based Layered Hybrid AI-Driven Knowledge Model for Personalized E-Learning. Mathematics 2026, 14, 808. https://doi.org/10.3390/math14050808

article_title: Lateral reading: College students learn to critically evaluate internet sources in an online course
citation: Breakstone, J., Smith, M., Connors, P., Ortega, T., Kerr, D., & Wineburg, S. (2021). Lateral reading: College students learn to critically evaluate internet sources in an online course. Harvard Kennedy School (HKS) Misinformation Review. https://doi.org/10.37016/mr-2020-56
title: Lateral reading: the professional fact checkers' strategy of leaving an unfamiliar site to consult the broader Web
description: Lateral reading is "the act of leaving an unknown website to consult other sources to evaluate the original site," derived from observations of professional fact checkers whose approaches were compared with those of undergraduates and history professors. While academics and students read vertically, staying on the target site, fact checkers "left it almost immediately and opened new tabs across the horizontal axis of their browser," answering who is behind the information, what the evidence is, and what other sources say. The article frames these as "fast and frugal" heuristics and builds its curriculum on them.
requirements: Consulting trusted sources from the broader Web rather than judging a site by its own surface features
constraints: Prior research showed students tend to evaluate a website by remaining on it without turning to the open Web, which motivated the emphasis on lateral reading
target_learners: College students
Middle school and high school students (per prior interventions the article cites)
target_learning_goals: Judging the credibility of unfamiliar online sources quickly and accurately
examples: Fact checkers in the underlying observational study evaluated unfamiliar websites with screens recorded, leaving sites to consult the broader Web

article_title: Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: a practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs
citation: Lakens, D. (2013). Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: a practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00863
title: Supplementary spreadsheet for effect size calculations
description: A supplementary spreadsheet accompanies the article "to make it as easy as possible for researchers to incorporate effect size calculations into their workflow." It calculates the effect sizes discussed (d-family standardizers including the common language effect size, Hedges' gav/grm, and η²G for commonly used designs), also provides the outcome of statistical tests, and recommends either Hedges's gav or Hedges's grm based on which value is most similar to Cohen's ds in a between-subjects design.
requirements: Researchers must enter the required statistics from their study (means, standard deviations, correlation or t-values) for the spreadsheet to compute the recommended effect sizes
constraints: The spreadsheet covers the t-test and ANOVA designs treated in the article, with η²G available only for commonly used experimental designs
target_learners: researchers reporting t-tests and ANOVAs
target_learning_goals: calculating and reporting effect sizes for power analyses and meta-analyses
examples: The article uses the spreadsheet in its illustrative example to obtain η²G = 0.26 and a common language effect size of 0.93 for correlated samples
key_sources: Lakens, D. (2013). Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: a practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00863

article_title: “Visual” Cortex Responds to Spoken Language in Blind Children
citation: Bedny, M., H. Richardson, and R. Saxe. (2015). "Visual" Cortex Responds to Spoken Language in Blind Children. Journal of Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1523/jneurosci.0634-15.2015
title: In the absence of visual input, spoken language colonizes the visual system during brain development
description: The article proposes that early in life, human cortex has a remarkably broad computational capacity, such that "the same cortical tissue can take on visual perception and language functions." In blindness, "spoken language colonizes the visual system during brain development," with language responses appearing early and remaining stable while sound responses grow with age. The account explains why occipital cortex in blind individuals responds to sound and spoken language.
requirements: Requires the absence of visual input from early in development for spoken language to colonize occipital cortex.
constraints: The account is drawn from a cross-sectional developmental sample of blind and sighted children aged 4–17.
target_learners: blind children and adolescents
target_learning_goals: cortical specialization for language in the absence of visual input
examples: Blind and sighted children aged 4–17 listened to stories and two auditory control conditions (unfamiliar foreign speech, and music) while occipital responses were measured.
key_sources: Bedny, M., H. Richardson, and R. Saxe. (2015). "Visual" Cortex Responds to Spoken Language in Blind Children. Journal of Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1523/jneurosci.0634-15.2015

article_title: A review of control processes and their locus in language switching
citation: Mathieu Declerck & Andrea M. Philipp. (2015). A review of control processes and their locus in language switching. Psychon Bull Rev. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-015-0836-1
title: Language switching paradigms: cued, alternating, voluntary, and sequence-based variants for studying language control
description: The review organizes language switching research around four paradigms that differ in how languages and concepts are cued: cued switching with visual language cues, alternating switching with predictable sequences, voluntary switching based on endogenous choices, and sequence-based language switching (SBLS) with memorized sequences and no visual cues or stimuli. The authors state that "a large variety of language switching paradigms with individual strengths and weaknesses can be used to study language control in language switching." Each paradigm affords different manipulations, such as time-based intervals in cued switching and switch-rate measures in voluntary switching.
requirements: Bilingual participants and a task in which languages must be produced or comprehended on separate trials, with switch and repetition trials distinguishable
constraints: Comprehension studies generally do not implement explicit visual language cues, so cued switching research is mainly production-based
target_learners: Bilinguals across proficiency levels, including second language learners and highly proficient bilinguals
target_learning_goals: Understanding mechanisms and loci of bilingual language control during speech production and comprehension
examples: Meuter and Allport's cued paradigm used digits as concepts and colored rectangles as language cues; SBLS used overlearned sequences such as weekdays or numbers with an auditory response signal
key_sources: Mathieu Declerck & Andrea M. Philipp. (2015). A review of control processes and their locus in language switching. Psychon Bull Rev. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-015-0836-1

article_title: A review of control processes and their locus in language switching
citation: Mathieu Declerck & Andrea M. Philipp. (2015). A review of control processes and their locus in language switching. Psychon Bull Rev. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-015-0836-1
title: Models of language control propose divergent loci: concept level, lemma level, and processing outside language processing
description: The review contrasts control models by their proposed functional locus. The inhibitory control model (Green, 1998) explains switch costs via reactive, persisting inhibition; the BIA family accounts for comprehension-based control via language nodes inhibiting competing words; and non-inhibitory models propose language-cue activation instead. The authors note "several loci of language control have been proposed, ranging from the concept level, lemma level, and a processing stage outside of language processing," and that several models propose more than one locus, both within and outside language processing.
requirements: A processing-stage architecture of language production or comprehension in which candidate loci (concept, lemma, phonology, orthography) can be distinguished empirically
constraints: The review's main focus is on behavioral results; nonbehavioral evidence is treated only in other reviews
target_learners: Bilinguals across proficiency levels
target_learning_goals: Understanding where in the language processing system control mechanisms operate during bilingual language switching
examples: In the modified ICM, language schemas activate language nodes whose inhibition targets lemmas of the non-target language; the BIA+ distinguishes a word identification system from a task/decision system outside language processing
key_sources: Mathieu Declerck & Andrea M. Philipp. (2015). A review of control processes and their locus in language switching. Psychon Bull Rev. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-015-0836-1

article_title: Deaf children's non-verbal working memory is impacted by their language experience
citation: Marshall C, Jones A, Denmark T, Mason K, Atkinson J, Botting N and Morgan G (2015) Deaf children's non-verbal working memory is impacted by their language experience. Front. Psychol. 6:527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00527
title: Language experience, not deafness per se, shapes non-verbal working memory development
description: The article proposes that the quality and timing of language exposure—regardless of modality—drives the development of non-verbal, executive-loaded working memory. As the authors state, "rich language experience from birth, and the good language skills that result from this early age of acquisition, play a critical role in the development of NVWM and in performance on NVWM tasks." The three-group design (hearing, native signers, non-native signers) teases apart auditory experience from language experience, since native signers have full language access without auditory input.
requirements: Comparison groups that differ in language experience but are matched on age and non-verbal reasoning, using non-verbal tasks requiring minimal verbal instruction
constraints: The authors note other developmental differences between native and non-native signers (parental attachment, attention-getting strategies, social-cognitive development) might work alongside language exposure; causal direction over developmental time remains unresolved
target_learners: deaf children aged 6–11 years
children acquiring language in suboptimal early environments
target_learning_goals: development of non-verbal executive-loaded working memory
examples: Native deaf signers (n = 8) exposed to BSL from birth did not differ from hearing children on executive-loaded NVWM tasks, while non-native signers did
key_sources: Marshall C, Jones A, Denmark T, Mason K, Atkinson J, Botting N and Morgan G (2015) Deaf children's non-verbal working memory is impacted by their language experience. Front. Psychol. 6:527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00527

article_title: Number processing and arithmetic skills in children with cochlear implants
citation: Pixner, S., Leyrer, M., and Moeller, K. (2014). Number processing and arithmetic skills in children with cochlear implants. Frontiers in Psychology 5:1479. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01479
title: Language-dependent place-value processing account of specific arithmetic difficulties in children with cochlear implants
description: The article adopts the view, following LeFevre et al.'s developmental model and the Triple Code model, that mastery of the base-10 place-value structure of the Arabic number system is language dependent. It uses this account to explain why children with CI, despite atypical language development, show qualitatively similar arithmetic performance but specific impairments exactly "when demands on place-value understanding" increase — in borrow subtraction and wider number-line ranges. The account holds that general verbal representations support arithmetic fact retrieval, while quantity and symbol representations are less language dependent.
requirements: The account presupposes atypical or delayed language development as the source of impaired place-value understanding, as in children with CI
constraints: The article did not measure language performance directly, comparing groups instead, and calls for future studies with a combined correlational approach to cross-validate the findings
target_learners: children with cochlear implants
typically developing elementary school children (grades 3–5)
target_learning_goals: place-value understanding of the Arabic base-10 number system
examples: Borrow subtraction problems and 0–1000 number line estimation were the two task conditions in which CI children's performance declined disproportionately relative to hearing peers

article_title: Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue
citation: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466
title: Three core tool classes of learning analytics: data capture and archiving, data analysis, and data representation and use
description: The article describes a core set of tools that LA contributes to learning research. "Tools for data capture and archiving" extract attributes of student behavior for later analysis, from stored text to real-time speech transcription, facial expression recognition, and eye-gaze tracking. "Tools for data analysis" apply specialized algorithms for search, retrieval, and pattern discovery to very large datasets. "Tools for data representation and use" make discovered patterns useful to researchers, teachers, and learners through new representations and responsive learning technologies.
requirements: Patterns discovered in the data must be made useful not only for researchers but also for teachers and learners, which requires new representations and technologies for each group.
target_learners: Researchers, teachers, and learners using analytics-informed learning environments
target_learning_goals: Capturing, analyzing, representing, and acting on patterns in learning process data
examples: A hypothetical online mathematics game project illustrates the tools: instrumenting the game, running machine learning over the logs, then displaying results to the teacher or students or driving real-time guidance.

article_title: Mutualistic Coupling Between Vocabulary and Reasoning Supports Cognitive Development During Late Adolescence and Early Adulthood
citation: Kievit, R. A., Lindenberger, U., Goodyer, I. M., Jones, P. B., Fonagy, P., Bullmore, E. T., the Neuroscience in Psychiatry Network, & Dolan, R. J. (2017). Mutualistic Coupling Between Vocabulary and Reasoning Supports Cognitive Development During Late Adolescence and Early Adulthood. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617710785
title: Latent change score modeling framework for comparing developmental theories
description: The article uses bivariate latent change score (LCS) models, which "conceptualize differences between successive measurements as latent change factors," allowing within-subject change to be modeled via self-feedback (β) and coupling (γ) parameters. This framework let the authors translate g-factor, investment, and mutualism accounts into competing psychometric models and compare them directly on the same longitudinal data — something prior studies had not done. The coupling parameter indexes whether change in one domain is affected by the prior level of the other domain.
requirements: At least two measurement occasions per participant; structural equation modeling software (lavaan was used)
constraints: With only two waves, lead-lag relations cannot be modeled; the authors note three or more waves would allow change scores to predict subsequent change scores
target_learners: adolescents and young adults in longitudinal cohort studies
target_learning_goals: quantifying cross-domain developmental dynamics in cognitive abilities
examples: Applied to WASI-II Matrix Reasoning and Vocabulary subtests from the NSPN cohort, with Time 2 scores rescaled for varying intertest intervals

article_title: The relation between language and arithmetic in bilinguals: insights from different stages of language acquisition
citation: Van Rinsveld A, Brunner M, Landerl K, Schiltz C and Ugen S (2015) The relation between language and arithmetic in bilinguals: insights from different stages of language acquisition. Front. Psychol. 6:265. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00265
title: Language-dependent exact arithmetic: verbal coding of arithmetic facts and verbal working memory in computation
description: The article frames exact arithmetic as relying on language at two levels: simple additions are retrieved as verbally coded arithmetic facts from memory, while complex additions require mental computations that rely on verbal working memory resources such as the phonological loop. The study tests this framework in bilinguals, where task language permeates instructions, presentation and answer production. As the authors state, "arithmetic facts are potentially represented or retrieved from memory in a verbal format and complex arithmetic solving processes rely at least partially on verbal working memory components."
requirements: Task language must permeate instructions, problem presentation and answer production to reveal language effects on arithmetic performance.
constraints: The framework was tested in German-French bilinguals who all acquired arithmetic in German within the Luxembourgish school system.
target_learners: Bilingual secondary-school students and young adults solving arithmetic problems in two languages
target_learning_goals: Exact arithmetic problem solving and arithmetic fact retrieval in a second language
examples: Participants solved 28 simple and 56 complex additions orally in separate German and French sessions, in visual and auditory presentation formats.

article_title: Predicting word reading and comprehension with executive function and speed measures across development: A latent variable analysis.
citation: Christopher, M. E., Miyake, A., Keenan, J. M., Pennington, B., DeFries, J. C., Wadsworth, S. J., Willcutt, E., & Olson, R. K. (2012). Predicting Word Reading and Comprehension with Executive Function and Speed Measures Across Development: A Latent Variable Analysis. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3360115/
title: Latent variable decomposition of shared versus unique cognitive predictors of separable reading constructs
description: The article's framework models word reading, reading comprehension, and listening comprehension as latent factors and asks which cognitive constructs predict their shared and unique variance. Latent variables represent "only what is common amongst the observed variables that define it, creating a more precise and 'pure' measure of the construct." Structural paths estimate how much change in a cognitive factor predicts change in a reading factor after controlling for correlated factors. The framework allowed the authors to test whether each of four cognitive abilities was a unique predictor and whether relations held across two age groups.
requirements: Multiple observed measures per latent construct to define each factor
Adequate sample size for confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling
constraints: The article states SEM modeling is correlational in nature and loadings should not be interpreted as suggesting that a change in the independent variable causes change in the dependent variable
target_learners: Children ages 8 to 16 learning to read and comprehend text
examples: The study used CFA to establish reading and cognitive factors, then SEM with structural paths from each cognitive factor to each reading factor, constrained across age groups

article_title: Knowledge is power: How conceptual knowledge transforms visual cognition
citation: Collins, Jessica A., & Olson, Ingrid R. (2014). Knowledge is Power: How Conceptual Knowledge Transforms Visual Cognition. Psychonomic bulletin & review. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-013-0564-3
title: Label-feedback hypothesis: labels act as modulators of a distributed interactive perceptual process
description: The review presents Lupyan's label-feedback hypothesis as a solution to the paradox that categorical perception is both robust (altering early perceptual processing) and fragile (mitigated by verbal working memory load). Language is treated not as a separate verbal module but as a modulator of a distributed interactive process: category-diagnostic perceptual features automatically activate labels, which feed back to amplify those features, enabling quick and transient modulation of perceptual representations.
requirements: Availability of verbal labels, which can be up- or down-regulated by linguistic manipulations such as verbal working memory load
constraints: The review notes an alternative account: left-lateralized categorical perception may reflect left-hemisphere propensity for category-level discriminations rather than language recruitment per se
target_learners: adult perceivers with established label systems
target_learning_goals: understanding how verbal labels shape perceptual discrimination learning
examples: Occupying verbal working memory interferes with categorical perception of color patches; non-linguistic categories also show categorical perception with left-hemisphere lateralization

article_title: American Sign Language Syntax and Analogical Reasoning Skills Are Influenced by Early Acquisition and Age of Entry to Signing Schools for the Deaf
citation: Henner J, Caldwell-Harris CL, Novogrodsky R and Hoffmeister R (2016) American Sign Language Syntax and Analogical Reasoning Skills Are Influenced by Early Acquisition and Age of Entry to Signing Schools for the Deaf. Front. Psychol. 7:1982. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.01982
title: Language experience as a continuum sensitive to maturational age
description: The article proposes that sign-language outcomes form a continuum reflecting cumulative language experience rather than a sharply closing critical window. As the authors state, "Our results demonstrate a continuum of outcomes that reﬂect experience with language as a continuous variable that is sensitive to maturational age." The best outcomes follow exposure from birth, then ASL exposure before age 6, then academic ASL exposure before 12, with the worst after age 12. The framework is used to advise parents to avoid all-or-none thinking about timing of sign language exposure.
requirements: Consistent, fully accessible exposure to ASL from peers and adults, as provided in signing school environments
constraints: The authors note considerable plasticity exists, so late exposure is not without benefit; outcomes depend on amount and timing of exposure
target_learners: Deaf children ages 7;6–18;5 in schools for the Deaf
examples: Ranking of outcomes by exposure timing: birth signing best, then entry before 6, then before 12, then after 12

article_title: Does speed of processing or vocabulary size predict later language growth in toddlers?
citation: Michelle S. Peter, Samantha Durrant, Andrew Jessop, Amy Bidgood, Julian M. Pine, Caroline F. Rowland. (2019). Does speed of processing or vocabulary size predict later language growth in toddlers? Cognitive Psychology 115 (2019) 101238. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2019.101238
title: Language 0–5 Project longitudinal cohort with looking-while-listening processing speed measurement
description: The Language 0–5 Project is a large longitudinal cohort in the North West of England from which this study draws its data. A total of 95 families were recruited, with a final sample of 90 contributing data at one or more measurement points. Children were tested in the laboratory at the University of Liverpool at 19, 25, and 31 months using a looking-while-listening paradigm with eye-tracking (EyeLink 1000 Plus), and caregivers completed repeated vocabulary checklists (UK-CDI, Lincoln CDI, CDI-III) between 8 and 37 months. The method is documented on the project's OSF site.
requirements: Caregivers completed vocabulary checklists in the week prior to lab visits or on paper during the session
constraints: Children with fewer than 25% good trials were excluded at each measurement point; RT was calculated only on distractor-initial trials where the child looked at the distracter at target word onset
target_learners: monolingual English-learning toddlers, born full-term and typically developing
examples: At 19 months children saw 64 test trials across two blocks with eight nouns each presented eight times as target; at 25 and 31 months adjective-noun combinations were added to increase challenge

article_title: Psychosocial Adversity in Early Childhood and Language and Literacy Skills in Adolescence: The Role of Speech-Language Pathology in Prevention, Policy, and Practice
citation: Pamela C. Snow. (2021). Psychosocial Adversity in Early Childhood and Language and Literacy Skills in Adolescence: The Role of Speech-Language Pathology in Prevention, Policy, and Practice. Perspectives of the ASHA Special Interest Groups. https://doi.org/10.1044/2020_PERSP-20-00120
title: The Language House framework linking social-emotional well-being, language, literacy, and academic achievement
description: The Language House (Snow, 2020) is a metaphorical schema, displayed in Figure 1, that "depicts the developmental links between social – emotional well-being, language and literacy development, and academic achievement, culminating in opportunities to participate in the social and economic mainstream." It provides a framework for speech-language pathologists to raise the profile of language and literacy difficulties among vulnerable children, for example when advocating to policy makers for underserved populations. It is also intended for raising clinicians' awareness of undocumented maltreatment histories affecting treatment engagement, and for preservice education to reinforce the developmental interplay across domains that clinical presentations do not map onto service delivery silos.
requirements: Use requires situating a child's language and literacy skills within their social-emotional and developmental history, including possible undocumented maltreatment
constraints: The article presents it as a metaphorical advocacy and education schema, not a tested predictive model
target_learners: Vulnerable children and adolescents with maltreatment histories
Preservice speech-language pathology students
target_learning_goals: Understanding developmental links between social-emotional well-being, language, literacy, and academic achievement
examples: The article proposes its use in advocating to policy makers for speech-language pathology services for underserved populations and in preservice SLP education

article_title: Some types of parent number talk count more than others: relations between parents’ input and children’s cardinal-number knowledge
citation: Gunderson Elizabeth A., Levine Susan C. (2011). Some types of parent number talk count more than others: Relations between parents' input and children's cardinal-number knowledge. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2011.01050.x
title: Large-number talk as a trigger for inducing the cardinal principle via representational discrepancy
description: The article proposes that children learn cardinal meanings of 1–3 by mapping number words onto the small-exact-number system, but cannot map large number words (4–10) onto either nonverbal system before learning the cardinal principle. Hearing large-number talk creates a "representational discrepancy" that motivates children to figure out what larger number words mean, and counting-and-labeling the same large set lets children notice that the cardinal label matches the last word of the count list. This explains why large-set present-object talk, though rare, is the strongest predictor of cardinal-number knowledge.
requirements: Exposure to number talk about sets of size 4 or greater, ideally with counting and labeling of the same present set
constraints: The account is stated as a hypothesis; the study is correlational and the authors call for experimental training studies to test it causally
target_learners: children aged roughly 14–46 months, prior to or during acquisition of the cardinal principle
target_learning_goals: learning the exact cardinal meanings of number words and the cardinal principle
examples: The article's example of count-plus-label talk about a large set: parents saying "there are four sticks, one, two, three, four" while the child can see the set
key_sources: Gunderson Elizabeth A., Levine Susan C. (2011). Some types of parent number talk count more than others: Relations between parents' input and children's cardinal-number knowledge. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2011.01050.x

article_title: The language and literacy development of young dual language learners: A critical review
citation: Hammer, C. S., Hoff, E., Uchikoshi, Y., Gillanders, C., Castro, D., & Sandilos, L. E. (2014). The Language and Literacy Development of Young Dual Language Learners: A Critical Review. Early childhood research quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2014.05.008
title: Language exposure and use as key influences on young DLLs' development
description: The review's organizing account of DLL development holds that the amount of language exposure to and usage of DLLs' two languages plays key roles in their language and literacy development. The review reports that differences in input amount explained DLL-monolingual accuracy differences in grammatical production, that processing efficiency tracks the language children hear more and know better, and that exposure timing (simultaneous versus sequential learning) shapes vocabulary trajectories. It concludes little is known about factors influencing DLL development, with exposure and usage the best-supported candidates.
requirements: Research designs must document children's amount of exposure to and usage of each language for the influence of input to be assessed
constraints: The review states little is known about factors that influence DLLs' development; the exposure-and-usage account is presented as preliminary given few areas with multiple studies
target_learners: Typically developing dual language learners from birth through age five
target_learning_goals: First- and second-language oral language development
examples: The review cites Bonnesen & Chilla (2011), Nicholls et al. (2011), and Paradis et al. (2010) attributing DLL-monolingual grammatical accuracy differences to amount of input in each language

The review cites Marchman et al. (2010) finding DLL toddlers faster at processing the language they heard more, with processing speed related to vocabulary size within a language but not across languages

article_title: Yes we can!
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2008). Yes we can! Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9055-3
title: Laurillard's framework distinguishing instructionist, social, constructionist and collaborative learning
description: A theoretical framework, presented by Diana Laurillard as a keynote-based paper, for distinguishing instructionist, social, constructionist and collaborative learning, whether computer-supported or not. The editor describes how it "spells out pedagogical needs" of collaborative learners — accessing explanations, posing questions, setting goals, repeating practice, reflecting, discussing, debating, articulating and documenting ideas — and thereby "provides a welcome basis for evaluating and comparing CSCL systems in terms of the important issues."
requirements: Technologies should be driven by the pedagogical requirements of collaborative learning rather than repurposed from business and leisure markets
constraints: As usually applied in classrooms, popular systems like smart-boards or Blackboard may not support specific desirable aspects of robust collaborative learning
target_learners: Collaborative learners in CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge building, questioning, reflecting, debating, and documenting ideas
examples: The editor suggests using the framework to argue that smart-boards or Blackboard, as usually applied in classrooms, do not support desirable aspects of robust collaborative learning, and to suggest new techniques including classroom practices.

article_title: Comparing metacognitive monitoring between native and non-native speaking primary school students
citation: Buehler, F. J., van Loon, M. H., Bayard, N. S., Steiner, M., & Roebers, C. M. (2021). Comparing metacognitive monitoring between native and non-native speaking primary school students. Metacognition and Learning, 16, 749–768. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09261-z
title: Language competencies as a theoretical basis for metacognitive monitoring development (Ebert's account as applied by the authors)
description: The article draws on a theoretical account in which language features support children's metacognition: "A grammatical understanding may support children to represent mental states," acquiring mental words may foster conceptual understanding of unobservable cognitive processes, and language skills may facilitate verbal interactions that foster learning about the mental world. On this basis, early language competencies have been related to later metacognition, motivating the hypothesis that native and non-native speaking children might differ in monitoring. The study's null results qualify this account for procedural monitoring resolution.
requirements: The account presupposes that monitoring is typically assessed verbally, so language of assessment may matter for measurement.
constraints: The study's own results suggest procedural monitoring resolution is relatively independent of the native language and language of assessment once instructions are understood; language abilities may be more closely related to declarative than procedural metacognition.
target_learners: Primary school children (~10-year-old fourth graders), including native and non-native speaking students
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive monitoring resolution (distinguishing correct from incorrect answers)
examples: The authors hypothesized that non-native speaking children's monitoring skills might be inferior based on this account, then tested and rejected that hypothesis in two studies.

article_title: Learning-by-Teaching Without Audience Presence or Interaction: When and Why Does it Work?
citation: Lachner, A., Hoogerheide, V., van Gog, T., & Renkl, A. (2022). Learning-by-Teaching Without Audience Presence or Interaction: When and Why Does it Work? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09643-4
title: Preliminary theoretical model of when and why learning by non-interactive teaching is effective
description: The review synthesizes its evidence on processes and boundary conditions into a preliminary theoretical model of when and why non-interactive teaching works. As the authors state: "We then synthesize the available empirical evidence on processes and boundary conditions to provide a preliminary theoretical model of when and why non-interactive teaching is effective." The model integrates the generative processing and social presence mechanisms with boundary conditions of modality, induced social presence, timing, teaching expectancy, prior knowledge, and ability beliefs, and is used to derive future research directions and recommendations for educational practice.
requirements: Studies implementing non-interactive teaching as an intervention with an experimental design and a peer-reviewed journal publication, per the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: The model is explicitly preliminary; the review states the available boundary-condition evidence should be considered preliminary because most studies did not explicitly test boundary conditions
target_learners: Students across age groups using non-interactive teaching as an individual study activity
target_learning_goals: Understanding and transfer of previously studied material through explaining it to an actual, remote, or imaginary audience

article_title: Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics
citation: Seyyed Kazem Banihashem, Dragan Gašević, Omid Noroozi, Halszka Jarodzka, Desiree Joosten-ten Brinke, Hendrik Drachsler. (2025). Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251370753
title: Use learning analytics to deliver scaled, real-time, personalized feedback that relieves teacher workload constraints on formative assessment
description: Because effective formative feedback must be timely and of sufficient quality, yet teachers face high workloads and large student populations, the review recommends leveraging learning analytics to scale feedback. It states: "This is also where learning analytics can significantly contribute to formative assessment by offering scaled, real-time, and personalized feedback." The review adds that learning analytics can make feedback manageable for busy teachers and provide real-time personalized reflections to both teachers and learners.
requirements: Feedback must remain well-designed, timely, ongoing, formatively useful, and easy to understand to be adequately valid
constraints: Automated tools may lack the nuance needed to assess complex thinking, potentially undermining educational intentions, as the review notes citing Bearman et al. (2023)
target_learners: higher education students
examples: The review cites studies where learning analytics monitored learning activities and provided real-time reflections and feedback to teachers and learners

article_title: Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement’s Directional Ordering
citation: Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement's Directional Ordering. Educational Psychology Review, 36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09887-w
title: Treat tests of contemporaneous (lag0) effects as a sensitivity analysis of whether panel-design time intervals are appropriate
description: Because effect sizes vary with the interval between measurement waves and there is no optimal interval, the article proposes testing lag0 paths within each wave as a practical check on design. "Tests of contemporaneous (lag0) effect in CLPMs are heuristic and offer a practical sensitivity analysis of whether the research design is based on appropriate time intervals." Significant lag0 effects may not be truly instantaneous but may signal that effects occur between waves, motivating shorter intervals; researchers should consider alternative intervals since failure to find lagged effects at one interval does not preclude effects at others.
requirements: Multi-wave panel data allowing both within-wave (lag0) and between-wave (lag1, lag2) reciprocal paths, and theoretical reasoning about the causal processes' temporality
constraints: Significant lag0 effects might reflect proximal events between waves rather than truly instantaneous causation; testing ever-shorter intervals with new data collections may not be feasible
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: appropriate longitudinal design and causal interpretation of self-concept-achievement relations
examples: The article's hypothetical model with waves falling between actual data waves illustrates how apparent lag0 effects may be proximal lag1 effects at unmeasured shorter intervals
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement's Directional Ordering. article_title: Bringing Assessment-to-Instruction (A2i) technology to scale: Exploring the process from development to implementation.
citation: Connor, Carol McDonald; May, Henry; Sparapani, Nicole; Hwang, Jin Kyoung; Adams, Ashley; Wood, Taffeta S.; Siegal, Sarah; Wolfe, Cassidy; Day, Stephanie. (2022). Bringing Assessment-to-Instruction (A2i) Technology to Scale: Exploring the Process from Development to Implementation. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000758
title: The Lattice Model of literacy development
description: The Lattice Model is the theoretical account underlying A2i that places instruction as a central force in students' literacy learning. Aligned with aptitude-by-treatment interactions, it holds that "the effect of instruction depends on each student’s linguistic, text-specific, cognitive, and social-emotional skills", so instructional effects differ by students' baseline skills across developmental domains. It further posits reciprocal, bi-directional effects: instruction improves literacy and linguistic, cognitive, and social-emotional skills, which in turn support literacy. This child-characteristics-by-instruction premise motivates individualizing instruction via A2i's algorithms.
requirements: Assessment information about individual students' language and literacy skills is needed so instruction can be matched to student characteristics
target_learners: kindergarten through third grade students, including English learners
examples: A2i's dynamic forecasting intervention algorithms compute recommended minutes of four instruction types based on individual students' language and literacy skills

article_title: Language experience matters for the emergence of early numerical concepts
citation: Stacee Santos, Hiram Brownell, Marie Coppola, Anna Shusterman and Sara Cordes. (2023). Language experience matters for the emergence of early numerical concepts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00202-w
title: Language access, rather than vocabulary ability, as the catalyst for the development of numerical abilities
description: The article proposes that the duration of a child's access to fluent linguistic input, indexed by Hearing Age, drives the emergence of both symbolic number knowledge and non-symbolic numerical discrimination. The authors state that "these ndings support our contention that language access (as measured by Hearing Age), rather than language ability (as measured by vocabulary), is a catalyst for re ning the development of numerical abilities." Possible mechanisms discussed include more number talk promoting attention to number (Spontaneous Focus on Number), while vocabulary alone did not capture the relevant experience.
requirements: A measure of cumulative duration of auditory access to spoken language, such as Hearing Age computed from hearing technology onset
Comparison samples differing in language access duration to test whether group effects persist
constraints: Hearing Age is a proxy that "only provides an estimate of the child's language access since birth but does not take into account the reduced access oral DHH children using auditory technology may experience on a day-to-day basis"
The sample was small, reflecting the low prevalence of congenital hearing loss, and could not explore how different hearing devices or levels of hearing account for performance
target_learners: preschool children (ages 3–6) acquiring early number concepts
oral deaf and hard-of-hearing children born to non-signing hearing parents
target_learning_goals: symbolic number knowledge (counting, number word knowledge via Give-N)
understanding of comparative quantity language (the word "more")
examples: The study computed a Hearing Age for each DHH child from the hearing questionnaire and replaced chronological age with it in regression models, finding group differences in the three numerical measures disappeared while vocabulary differences persisted

article_title: Insights from 200+ years of personalized learning
citation: David Dockterman. (2018). Insights from 200 + years of personalized learning. npj Science of Learning 3:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0033-x
title: The Lancasterian (Monitorial) System as an early competency-based, self-paced, peer-learning model
description: The article describes the early-nineteenth-century Monitorial System created by John Lancaster as a scalable instructional organization predating modern personalized learning. Children were placed along learning progressions per domain, with student monitors delivering "scripted lessons to develop skills and assessments to move each student to the next level in the sequence as soon as he demonstrated mastery." The author writes, "Today we might call what Lancaster devised 200 years ago a self-paced, mastery-based, peer-learning instructional system," noting its similarity to current competency-based visions.
requirements: A scalable, accountable mechanism for organizing masses of students with an affordable cadre of teachers, as the article states drove its creation
constraints: The article states the competency-based organizing principle "turned out to be too much of an organizational burden for urban schools" as populations grew
target_learners: mass public school students in the early nineteenth century
target_learning_goals: foundational reading, writing, and math mastery
examples: Lancaster published books guiding uniform implementation, and the system spread across the United States and other nations in the early nineteenth century

article_title: Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education
citation: Julien Broisin, Rémi Venant & Philippe Vidal. (2017). Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 27:154–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0079-3
title: Lab4CE remote laboratory environment
description: Lab4CE is a remote laboratory for computer education built on a "three-layered architecture inspired from the iLab shared architecture": a laboratory layer implementing OpenStack for virtual machine management at scale, a middleware layer with RESTful core services and an Elasticsearch-based learning analytics store, and a learning layer hosting rich pedagogical interfaces. It distinguishes an experiment (a teacher-defined specification of virtual resources and pedagogical objectives) from a practical session (a learner-owned instantiation), and integrates scaffolding tools intended to increase engagement in remote practical activities.
requirements: Existing virtualization tools (OpenStack as IaaS) plus middleware services mapping experiments and practical sessions onto OpenStack artifacts with role-based access control
constraints: The web Terminal control interface restricts practice to computer science topics that do not require a graphical interface
target_learners: undergraduate computer science students and their tutors
target_learning_goals: system and network administration, programming, database management skills
examples: In the study, a simple experiment with a single Linux computer let each of 139 students access their own virtual machine from anywhere

article_title: Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education
citation: Julien Broisin, Rémi Venant & Philippe Vidal. (2017). Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 27:154–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0079-3
title: Lab4CE micro authoring tool for experiment design
description: An authoring tool for instructors that addresses the micro learning design capacity the authors find lacking in other remote labs such as Go-Lab's Graasp.eu. Designers first fill a form specifying learning metadata (name, description, pedagogical objective, availability period), then design the experiment's topology at two granularity levels by dragging Computer, Router and Switch components, each with adaptable default software configurations. Publication translates the configuration into OpenStack format, guaranteeing "independence between the authoring tool and the virtualization software".
requirements: Virtual resources must be configurable to the specific discipline taught, e.g. a programming language must be installed and configured on the remote lab
constraints: Experiments are specifications only; the authoring tool does not deploy resources, which are created on demand when learners start a practical session
target_learners: instructors and instructional designers of remote computer science experiments
target_learning_goals: configuration and re-engineering of online experiments aligned with pedagogical objectives
examples: The illustrated scenario designed an IP-configuration experiment with four computers, two switches and one router, and constraints such as Stations 1 & 2 in the same subnet
key_sources: Julien Broisin, Rémi Venant & Philippe Vidal. (2017). Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 27:154–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0079-3

article_title: Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education
citation: Julien Broisin, Rémi Venant & Philippe Vidal. (2017). Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 27:154–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0079-3
title: Artifact-awareness tool for shared practical sessions
description: A component of Lab4CE's rich learning interface operationalizing artifact awareness, defined in the article as "one person's up-to-the-moment knowledge of the artifacts and tools that other distributed people are using as they perform their individual, ongoing work". It shows users involved in an experiment with role and connection status icons, supports inviting peers or tutors into a practical session, displays partners' Terminals as live-feed thumbnails, and highlights with a light red line when another user performs an action on a shared resource. The middleware proxies and broadcasts interactions in real time to the session's owner and guests.
requirements: The middleware layer must act as a proxy between users and virtual resources so interactions can be captured and broadcast in real time
constraints: Unlike VNC-based or video-based solutions, it requires no additional software on users' hosts; in computer education audio/video feeds are worthless since no physical changes occur on the computer
target_learners: learners and tutors engaged in collaborative remote practical sessions
target_learning_goals: awareness of who is working on what during collaborative practical work
examples: In the illustrated scenario, Julien and Rémi working on Station 2 see each other's Terminal thumbnails and the red line marking a guest's action
key_sources: Julien Broisin, Rémi Venant & Philippe Vidal. (2017). Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 27:154–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0079-3

citation: Julien Broisin, Rémi Venant & Philippe Vidal. (2017). Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 27:154–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0079-3
title: Lab4CE learning analytics tool and management dashboard
description: Two analytics artifacts for tutors. The learning analytics tool visualizes, per virtual resource, a timeline of all recorded activities — commands with date, string and output, and chat posts from public and private rooms — with color-coded nodes, filters and zoom; it supports "monitoring of students' activities, (a)synchronous guidance and assistance, evaluation of learners' performances, or identification of learners who face challenges". The management dashboard built on Horizon monitors the computational status and configuration of each learner's virtual resources so tutors can initiate a chat if something seems wrong.

constraints: The ready-to-use Horizon dashboard is designed for cloud monitoring and does not provide fine-grained information such as the software embedded in a virtual resource or network routing tables; a learning-oriented dashboard is work in progress
target_learners: tutors monitoring remote practical sessions, and learners reviewing their own or peers' sessions
target_learning_goals: tutoring support, performance evaluation, identification of learners facing difficulties
examples: Tutors can record a near-perfect session into the store and reuse it to demonstrate the best solution for a given experiment

article_title: The Impacts of Domain-General vs. Domain-Specific Diagramming Tools on Writing
citation: Barstow, B., Fazio, L., Lippman, J., Falakmasir, M., Schunn, C. D., & Ashley, K. D. (2017). The Impacts of Domain-General vs. Domain-Specific Diagramming Tools on Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 27, 671–693. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0130-z
title: LASAD-based argument diagramming intervention with SWoRD peer review for research paper introductions
description: The intervention used LASAD, "an online diagramming tool that allows users to create visual representations of arguments, including both the elements of an argument and their relationships," customized with two frameworks (domain-general and psychology-specific). Students trained on a model diagram in pairs, built diagrams justifying their hypotheses, received blind peer review of their diagrams through the SWoRD system from four reviewers, revised, and used TF feedback to draft introductions. Survey data showed most students found LASAD easy to use and used their diagrams and peer comments when writing, but found peer ratings much less useful.
requirements: Teaching fellows require training, as one TF who did not attend training and another who altered the assignment had their sections' data excluded
constraints: Students struggled to understand peers' diagrams, so peer comments were often superficial or off-target; only 50% found peer comments helpful and 20% found ratings helpful
target_learners: undergraduates in small lab sections of a psychology research methods course
target_learning_goals: constructing arguments for hypotheses supported by relevant, opposing, and validity-considered citations
examples: The psychology-specific framework required relevance (close, medium, far, unsure) and validity (strong, medium, weak, unsure) ratings with justifications on Supports and Opposes links
