article_title: First-Year Engineering Students’ Strategies for Taking Exams
citation: Jakub Kuzilek, Zdenek Zdrahal, Jonas Vaclavek, Viktor Fuglik, Jan Skocilas, Annika Wolff. (2023). First-Year Engineering Students' Strategies for Taking Exams. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00303-4
title: Layered Markov chain method transforming exam attempt logs into probabilistic graphs
description: The article introduces "the method - which transforms the student exam attempt log into a probabilistic graphical representation". Exam attempts are aggregated to six exam-period weeks, encoded as quaternary states over three courses (64 states per week, state space of 384), and used to build non-homogeneous layered Markov chains with absorbing final-week states. Graph complexity is measured with a polynomial-based average complexity measure, and graphs are compared with a normalized shortest-path kernel. Edges taken by more than 10% of a group are extracted to reveal predominant patterns.
requirements: Exam attempt logs with dates, courses and outcomes for each student
A predefined exam period divided into weeks and a fixed set of exam courses
constraints: The Markov property means the model works with no memory and cannot provide more complex information about the process
Complexity comparison across graphs with different state sets requires a simulation study the authors did not carry out
target_learners: first-year university students
target_learning_goals: exam planning and time management during exam periods
examples: The method is demonstrated on 311 FME students in 2017/2018, e.g. example student 15456106's log transforming to the state sequence <1, 1, 1, 3, 15, 63>

article_title: Teachers’ perceptions of the usability of learning analytics reports in a flipped university course: when and how does information become actionable knowledge?
citation: Anouschka van Leeuwen. (2019). Teachers’ perceptions of the usability of learning analytics reports in a flipped university course: when and how does information become actionable knowledge? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-018-09639-y
title: Design principles for learning analytics as teacher support: coordination, comparison, and customization
description: The article adopts, from Wise and Vytasek (2017), three design principles that make LA an effective support tool for teachers: "coordination, i.e., making the LA an integral part of the educational context", "comparison, i.e., providing a frame of reference to interpret the meaning of an analytic", and "customization, i.e., the recognition that each situation requires specific LA". The study's own findings are interpreted through these principles, for example teachers' use of the course average as the comparison baseline.
requirements: LA must be coordinated with the educational context so reports are part of the teaching routine
constraints: The principles are attributed to Wise and Vytasek (2017), a theoretical discussion, not tested empirically in this study
target_learners: university teachers in flipped/blended courses
target_learning_goals: monitoring and adapting to student learning processes
examples: The weekly LA reports were handed out on paper during the Monday staff meeting, coordinating the analytics with the existing team routine

article_title: Learning analytics in inquiry-based learning: a systematic review
citation: Fan Chen, Gaowei Chen. (2025). Learning analytics in inquiry-based learning: a systematic review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10507-9
title: Dual-role account of learning analytics in inquiry-based learning
description: The review frames LA in IBL as playing two complementary roles. First, LA provides "data-supported analysis to uncover student engagement and performance during inquiry activities", including assessing engagement levels, identifying learning patterns or challenges, and evaluating inquiry skills like formulating testable hypotheses. Second, "LA-driven insights serve as supportive tools that provide real-time feedback and targeted intervention" for students while assisting teachers in improving IBL design and implementation. The review uses this dual-role framing to organise its analysis of how LA both understands inquiry processes and supports students and teachers across inquiry stages.
requirements: LA in IBL requires process data collection and analysis, such as behaviour logs, discussion transcripts, and multimodal data, to generate actionable insights for students and teachers.
constraints: The review notes limited understanding of how LA has been used to understand students' inquiry processes at specific stages, and limited research on the effectiveness of LA tools as interventions.
target_learners: K-12 students
university students
teachers
examples: The review cites Dickler et al. (2021) employing teacher-facing dashboards to scaffold students' inquiry through discursive supports, and de Araujo et al. (2024) using LA-based conversational agents to foster productive discourse during IBL tasks.

citation: Korving, H., Hernández, M. & De Groot, E. (2016). Look at me and pay attention! A study on the relation between visibility and attention in weblectures. Computers and Education, vol. 94, pp. 151-161. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.11.011
title: Use a large lecturer video for weblectures longer than 15 minutes; use large slides for shorter weblectures
description: Based on the finding that the effect of visibility on reported attention depends on watching duration, the article recommends that for weblectures longer than 15 minutes a large video of the lecturer supports attention, while for shorter weblectures a large image of the slides is preferable. The authors state: "students report more attention after watching a large video of a lecturer and a small image of slides when listening to a lecture for more than 15 min. constraints: The effect was demonstrated with 7.5-minute clips, and the authors note results might not be similar for full-length weblectures.

article_title: Effect of Strategy Teaching for the Solution of Ratio Problems on Students' Proportional Reasoning Skills
citation: Şen, C., & Güler, G. (2017). Effect of Strategy Teaching For the Solution of Ratio Problems on Students' Proportional Reasoning Skills. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Sciences, 5(2). https://www.moj-es.net
title: Langrall and Swafford's four levels of proportional reasoning
description: The article adopts a four-level developmental framework for scoring proportional reasoning: Level 0 is the "Absence of proportional reasoning", where students make baseless predictions and additive rather than multiplicative comparisons; Level 1 is informal reasoning about proportional states using pictures, models or concrete materials; Level 2 is quantitative reasoning using unitizing, unit ratios, change multiplier, equivalent fractions and cross-multiplication; Level 3 is formal reasoning with precise and accurate language. The researchers used these levels to classify and grade all PRT and homework answers, mapping scores into very low, low, medium and high bands over a 0-20 interval.
requirements: Answers must be classified and graded against the defined levels, with researcher concordance checks (94%-100% in this study)
constraints: Applied to sixth-grade students' responses to six ratio problem states scored within one 40-minute course hour
target_learners: sixth-grade secondary school students
examples: The researchers scored the 6-item PRT from 0-20, classifying 0-5 as very low, 6-10 as low, 11-15 as medium, and 16-20 as high.

article_title: Learning from Cluster Randomized Trials in Education: An Assessment of the Capacity of Studies to Determine "What Works," "For Whom," and "Under What Conditions"
citation: Jessaca Spybrook, Qi Zhang, Ben Kelcey, Nianbo Dong. (2020). Learning From Cluster Randomized Trials in Education: An Assessment of the Capacity of Studies to Determine What Works, For Whom, and Under What Conditions. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373720929018
title: Design CRTs seeking to answer for whom with larger numbers of students per school, since total individuals drive individual-level moderator power
description: The article's design recommendation for efficacy trials aiming at moderator questions: because the total number of individuals, not clusters, drives power for individual-level moderators, planners should increase students per cluster. As the article states, "if a study is seeking to answer not only what works but also for whom, larger numbers of students per school will be helpful in answering the for whom question." This is feasible because standardized assessment makes added students inexpensive.
requirements: A nested two- or three-level CRT design with individual-level moderators of interest
Planned sample sizes known at the design phase for power calculations
constraints: Increasing students per cluster is less feasible for pre-K studies or special populations relying on costly individual test administration
Recruiting additional schools to power school-level moderators is very costly and likely outside one study's budget
target_learners: pre-K through grade 12 students in efficacy trials
target_learning_goals: rigorous evidence about for whom and under what conditions educational interventions work
examples: The 37 sampled CRTs were power-analyzed using planned sample sizes from structured abstracts; studies randomizing elementary, middle, or high schools with large numbers of students per school showed MDESDIND smaller than MDES, while pre-K studies with 10 or fewer students per teacher could not detect small moderators
key_sources: Jessaca Spybrook, Qi Zhang, Ben Kelcey, Nianbo Dong. (2020). Learning From Cluster Randomized Trials in Education: An Assessment of the Capacity of Studies to Determine What Works, For Whom, and Under What Conditions. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373720929018

article_title: Improving Critical Thinking Skills Using Learning Model Logan Avenue Problem Solving (LAPS)-Heuristic
citation: Desi Anggrianto, Madziatul Churiyah, Mohammad Arief. (2016). Improving Critical Thinking Skills Using Learning Model Logan Avenue Problem Solving (LAPS)-Heuristic. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.9. https://www.iiste.org
title: LAPS-Heuristic: a constructivist problem-solving learning model
description: LAPS-Heuristic is a constructivist, student-centered learning model in which "students in solving problems by questioning what the problem is, whether any other alternative solutions, whether it is beneficial, if the solution, and how effective to solve it." Its stages are analyzing and understanding the problem, designing and planning a solution, looking for a solution, and examining the solution. The article applies it to vocational economics content to train critical thinking through group discussion and presentation of solutions.
requirements: Students must be exposed to varied problems and work through discussion and presentation activities so problem-solving becomes habitual
constraints: Students unfamiliar with problem solving need extra teacher direction and guidance at first application
The model requires more time allocation than conventional learning because of small-group and large-group discussion plus presentations
target_learners: vocational high school (SMK) class X students
examples: In the experimental class, students were continuously faced with problems and required to find solutions through discussion and presentation activities on demand and supply curve material.
key_sources: Desi Anggrianto, Madziatul Churiyah, Mohammad Arief. (2016). Improving Critical Thinking Skills Using Learning Model Logan Avenue Problem Solving (LAPS)-Heuristic. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.9. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1095745

citation: Desi Anggrianto, Madziatul Churiyah, Mohammad Arief. (2016). Improving Critical Thinking Skills Using Learning Model Logan Avenue Problem Solving (LAPS)-Heuristic. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.9. https://www.iiste.org
title: LAPS-Heuristic lesson pattern: understand, plan, solve, and examine a problem through group discussion and presentation
description: The lesson pattern sequences learning around a problem cycle: "analyzing and understanding the problem, designing and planning a solution, looking for a solution of the problem, and examining the solution." Students work in small-group discussion, then present results to other groups and compare alternative solutions. The article reports this pattern triggered reasoning activity that includes basic, critical, and creative thinking.
requirements: Problems must be varied so students encounter new problems to solve
Group discussion must be followed by presentation to other groups
constraints: Early meetings require patient teacher directing and guiding because students are unfamiliar with the syntax
target_learners: vocational high school students in business and management
examples: The experimental class lesson plans (RPP) for LAPS-Heuristic on curve and equilibrium of demand and supply material implemented this cycle over the taught sessions.

article_title: Effects of Prior Knowledge of Topics and the Instructional Objectives on Students' Achievement in Literature-in-English
citation: Mbah, B. A. (2015). Effects of prior knowledge of topics and the instructional objectives on students' achievement in Literature-in-English. Journal of Education and Practice, 6(20). http://www.iiste.org
title: Literature-in-English Achievement Test (LAT)
description: The LAT is a researcher-designed 35-item objective test with four options (A-D) per item, one correct and three distractors. Section A contains fourteen items on African prose, Section B thirteen items on African drama, and Section C eight items on African poetry. It was validated by specialists and "A reliability coefficient of 0.89 was obtained using Richardson formula (KR.20)". It served as the pretest and posttest instrument, with items reshuffled for the posttest.
requirements: Validation by specialists in Literature-in-English, Language Education, and Measurement and Evaluation
target_learners: senior secondary school class two (SS II) students
examples: Administered as a pretest at the onset of the six-week experiment and as a posttest after items were reshuffled and typed on a different colour of paper

article_title: Effect of Guided Inquiry Teaching Method on Secondary School Students' Achievement in Light and Sound Waves in Abuja, Nigeria
citation: Ekomaye, Daniel Gideon (2019). Effect of Guided Inquiry Teaching Method on Secondary School Students’ Achievement in Light and Sound Waves in Abuja, Nigeria. Journal of Education and e-Learning Research, 6(2): 82-87. https://doi.org/10.20448/journal.509.2019.62.82.87

description: LASWAT is a researcher-developed instrument of "50 multiple choice test items" used to collect both pre-test and post-test scores; after the pre-test the questions and options were reshuffled and the paper colour changed from white to yellow. Three experts validated it, yielding "A validity index of 0.86", and test-retest with Kudar-Richardson formula 20 established "a reliability coefficient of 0.87". Item analysis covered difficulty index, discriminating index and distractors' analysis.

target_learners: SS2 secondary school physics students in Abuja, Nigeria
target_learning_goals: Achievement in light and sound waves
examples: Used as pre-test before instruction and post-test after the treatment period for both experimental and control groups

article_title: Effect of Layered Curriculum in Problem Solving Skills of Students in Science and Technology Course
citation: Koc Akran, S., & Gurbuzturk, O. (2019). Effect of layered curriculum in problem solving skills of students in science and technology course. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 5(1), 135-150. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.5.1.147
title: Layered Curriculum as a three-layer C-B-A differentiation framework
description: Layered Curriculum, developed by Nunley, divides a unit into three layers: "C Layer: Basic knowledge", "B Layer: Application" and "A Layer: Critical thinking". Students choose activities within each layer according to their own learning style, must reach a points threshold (65-70 points in layer C) to progress, and give an oral defense explaining where they had difficulty. In this study the framework was implemented in a five-week Human Body Systems unit with task lists handed to experimental students in advance.
requirements: Units must be divided into C, B and A layers with different assignments in each layer
Students must be given freedom to choose which activities to perform
An oral defense is used to understand in which layer the student had difficulty
constraints: In this study the framework was applied to a 6th-grade Science and Technology unit over five weeks in one elementary school
target_learners: 6th grade elementary students
target_learning_goals: science content learning in the Human Body Systems unit
examples: Task lists assigned 10-point C-layer activities such as summarizing newspaper articles on blood donation, 15-point B-layer activities such as writing a poem about the heart, and 15-point A-layer activities such as designing an original model displaying blood transfusion
key_sources: Koc Akran, S., & Gurbuzturk, O. (2019). Effect of layered curriculum in problem solving skills of students in science and technology course. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 5(1), 135-150. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.5.1.147

citation: Rashida G. Gabdrakhmanova and Aleksandr Y. Kostarev. (2016). Pedagogical Modeling of the Competitive Activity of Athletes in Russian Lapta. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(13), 6090-6101. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: Three-level model characteristics of lapta play activity (minimum, stage, reference)
description: On the basis of the observational data the authors designed model characteristics of play activity at three qualification levels: "A minimum model shows the indicators of youth teams of low qualification, stage model reflects performance of play activity of teams of medium qualification; the reference model is based on the analysis of the play activity of the leading teams in Russia, that is, highly skilled teams." These models allow comprehensive assessment of success of players of different specializations and adjustment of the training process.
requirements: Data research of competitive activity as the basis for designing the model characteristics
constraints: Built from analysis of Russian lapta teams specifically
target_learners: lapta players of different skills and specializations
target_learning_goals: objective assessment of fitness and control of improvement of technical and tactical skills
examples: Used to make appropriate adjustments in the training process of lapta players

article_title: Evaluating the Effects of Mother Tongue on Math and Science Instruction
citation: Behrmann, T. (2018). Evaluating the effects of mother tongue on math and science instruction. Monument, CO, USA: ISTES Organization. https://www.istes.org
title: Language-as-medium framework: language is the key tool through which students process, express, and socially negotiate understanding
description: The article organizes its argument around the claim that the language of instruction is central to learning: as Benson is quoted, "language is clearly the key to communication and understanding in the classroom". Drawing on Vygotsky's sociocultural theory and Chomsky's views on language acquisition, the framework holds that children develop concepts, seek clarification, and express understanding through language, so instructing in a language students do not master forces simultaneous language learning and content learning. The study applies this framework by manipulating the medium of instruction (Kreyol vs French) in math and science lessons.
requirements: The medium of instruction must be a language students know well enough to communicate needs and process new concepts
constraints: The article notes the framework's application is complicated in Haiti by attitudes that treat Kreyol as unsuitable for academic purposes
target_learners: Haitian secondary students, primarily monolingual Kreyol speakers
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of math and science concepts
examples: The article quotes Chomsky's view that the most effective learning happens when people learn in their native tongues, and Vygotsky's account of language as a tool for social interaction
key_sources: Behrmann, T. (2018). Evaluating the effects of mother tongue on math and science instruction. Monument, CO, USA: ISTES Organization. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED603513

article_title: The Effects of Professional Development Initiatives on EFL Teachers' Degree of Self Efficacy
citation: Mohammad Nabi Karimi. (2011). The Effects of Professional Development Initiatives on EFL Teachers' Degree of Self Efficacy. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, Vol 36, 6, May 2011.
title: Policy makers should launch quality professional development programs aimed at raising teachers' operational knowledge and content standards to boost teacher efficacy
description: Based on the finding that multi-model PD significantly raised EFL teachers' efficacy beliefs, the article recommends that "educational policy makers should consider launching quality professional development programs aimed specifically at raising teachers' operational knowledge and content standards which in turn boosts the teachers' efficacy." The recommendation rests on the argument that enhanced efficacy judgments positively affect persistence, instructional success, commitment, and adoption of innovative strategies.
requirements: PD activities must be planned properly and address teachers' needs in all three components of teacher self-efficacy
constraints: The supporting evidence comes from a single quasi-experiment with 60 teachers; the article calls for larger samples, different groups, various settings, and longitudinal approaches
target_learners: in-service EFL teachers
examples: The study delivered PD through three 16-session courses combining five PD models for treatment teachers
key_sources: Mohammad Nabi Karimi. (2011). The Effects of Professional Development Initiatives on EFL Teachers' Degree of Self Efficacy. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, Vol 36, 6, May 2011. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ936991

article_title: The Effect of the Layered Curriculum on the 6th Grade Students' Learning Styles in Science Lesson
citation: Koc Akran, S., & Uzum, B. (2018). The effect of the layered curriculum on the 6th grade students' learning styles in Science lesson. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 4(3), 141-152. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.4.3.141
title: Nunley's layered curriculum: a three-layer (C-B-A) differentiated curriculum model
description: The layered curriculum, developed by K. F. Nunley, organizes teaching into three layers. Layer C is "the lowest layer in which all the students are required to be successful, and it includes basic knowledge and abilities", with many point-valued activities of which students complete 65-70 points' worth. Layer B contains application activities worth 15 points each, and Layer A, the highest layer, requires critical analysis, questioning and an original learning product. Students choose activities, keep them in a progress file, and are graded by criteria matched to layer difficulty.
requirements: An activities list prepared in accordance with the C, B and A layers, with points assigned by difficulty
A learning-teaching environment in which the teacher guides, monitors, directs and grades rather than lectures throughout
constraints: Students are not required to complete all Layer C activities; original products are required only in Layer A
target_learners: 6th grade secondary school science students
examples: In this study the experimental class worked through Layer C activities such as posters, crosswords and experiments, Layer B activities such as writing poems and preparing booklets, and Layer A original products

article_title: Approaches to Incorporating Late Pretests in Experiments: Evaluation of Two Early Mathematics and Self-Regulation Interventions
citation: Unlu, F., Layzer, C., Clements, D., Sarama, J., & Cook, D. (2013). Approaches to Incorporating Late Pretests in Experiments: Evaluation of Two Early Mathematics and Self-Regulation Interventions. SREE Fall 2013 Conference. https://www.sree.org/conferences/2013f/
title: Late pretest decontamination procedure producing predicted pretests free of early treatment effects
description: A three-step statistical procedure for removing early treatment effects from contaminated pretests. It entails building a model with the contaminated pretest as outcome and exogenous covariates plus time between school start and baseline testing as predictors, estimating it on control students only, and then "creating predicted pretests for all students using the estimated model but setting the time between school start and pretest date to zero." The article applies it in a preschool cluster RCT and says it can be applied in similar situations with exogenous predictors of the pretest.
requirements: Requires exogenous predictors of the pretest measures, including covariates collected before treatment and a measure of time between school start and baseline testing.
constraints: In the preliminary application, the predictors (student demographics and school characteristics) did not predict pretest measures well, so the corrected pretests did not improve precision.
target_learners: 4-year-old preschool children in early childhood centers and schools
examples: Applied in a three-armed cluster RCT of Building Blocks and BBSSR, with corrected pretests aggregated to the school level and used in ANCOVA impact models.
key_sources: Unlu, F., Layzer, C., Clements, D., Sarama, J., & Cook, D. (2013). Approaches to Incorporating Late Pretests in Experiments: Evaluation of Two Early Mathematics and Self-Regulation Interventions. SREE Fall 2013 Conference. https://www.sree.org/conferences/2013f/

article_title: The Effect of Laboratory Training Model of Teaching and Traditional Method on Knowledge, Comprehension, Application, Skills-Components of Achievement, Total Achievement and Retention Level in Chemistry
citation: Alireza Badeleh. (2011). The Effect of Laboratory Training Model of Teaching and Traditional Method on Knowledge, Comprehension, Application, Skills-Components of Achievement, Total Achievement and Retention Level in Chemistry. i-manager's Journal of School Educational Technology, Vol. 7, No. 1. https://www.imanagerpublications.com
title: Laboratory Training Model of Teaching (LTM)
description: The Laboratory Training Model of teaching is an approach in which "the learner practically experiences a specific concept with specific materials and equipments". Nothing is directly taught; the learning situation and conditions are provided so learners find solutions themselves, with the instructor circulating, asking and answering questions and guiding learning. It can be combined with group and discovery learning, and the article evaluates it against the teacher-centred traditional lecture method in chemistry.
requirements: A laboratory environment with materials and equipment for first-hand experimentation
An instructor circulating among students to guide, question and prevent students from getting stranded and discouraged
constraints: The article reports LTM is not as suitable for teaching non-experimental and lower-level components such as knowledge as it is for higher-level and experimental concepts
target_learners: Seventh-standard (lower secondary) science students
target_learning_goals: Chemistry achievement across knowledge, comprehension, application and skills
examples: Four chemistry chapters (Nature and Composition of Matter, Water, Heat, Acid Bases and Salts) were taught over 21 sessions per class via LTM or traditional lecture in two Mysore schools

article_title: Effect of Blended Learning Educational Model on Secondary School Students' Mathematics Conceptual Understanding
citation: Abdissa, D. G., Duressa, G. F., Olkaba, T. T., & Feyissa, E. G. (2024). Effect of blended learning educational model on secondary school students' mathematics conceptual understanding. Problems of Education in the 21st Century, 82(5), 585–599. https://doi.org/10.33225/pec/24.82.585
title: Lab-rotation blended learning via Google Classroom for secondary mathematics
description: The article's intervention combines face-to-face mathematics teaching with online learning through the Google Classroom LMS in a lab rotation arrangement. The online platform provided "lesson distribution, feedback gathering, assignments, and discussion forums" designed to support conventional in-person instruction. The experimental group experienced this model over 20 weeks totaling 27 hours (about 1.35 hours per week), while using the same course materials as the comparison group. Teachers received ten days of training covering online teaching, technology integration, and the platform.
requirements: School computer labs with internet access, teachers trained in online teaching and the Google Classroom platform, and student email accounts for platform login
constraints: The article notes blended learning was mainly implemented in higher education and not yet practiced in Ethiopian secondary schools, and that preparing online materials is time-consuming for educators
target_learners: Grade 10 secondary school students in Ethiopia
examples: Students joined a researcher-led Google Classroom via an invitation link and passcode, then interacted with instructional content online alongside in-person sessions

article_title: The Formation of Learners' Motivation to Study Physics in Terms of Sustainable Development of Education in Ukraine
citation: Igor Korsun. (2017). The Formation of Learnersí Motivation to Study Physics in Terms of Sustainable Development of Education in Ukraine. Journal of Teacher Education for Sustainability, vol. 19, no. 1, pp. 117ñ128. https://doi.org/10.1515/jtes-2017-0008
title: Five-step scheme of interest formation from situational to individual interest
description: The article adopts Lanina's (1985) scheme for the formation of learners' interest in physics, which proceeds through the steps "curiosity ñ active curiosity ñ attempts to understand ñ strong knowledge ñ scientific research". Situational interest begins to form at the first step, curiosity, and turns into active curiosity as learners show the increasing importance of the object for their interest. The step "strong knowledge" is where individual interest begins to form, and the final step, "scientific research", is the highest stage during which learners formulate their own tasks and solve them. The article uses this scheme to show the transition from a situational interest to an individual interest.
requirements: Learners progress through the steps in sequence, from curiosity to scientific research
constraints: The scheme is analyzed specifically for the formation of learners' interest in physics in the context of sustainable development of education
target_learners: secondary school learners aged 15ñ17 studying physics
target_learning_goals: formation of learners' interest in physics as a school subject and as a science

article_title: Latinos: Higher Education and Technology
citation: Sylvia L. Flores & Luis A. Flores. (2018). Latinos: Higher Education and Technology. Journal of Learning in Higher Education, 14(1). https://www.aabri.com/copyright.html
title: Small-scale meta-analysis of literature on Latinos, technology, and academic success in higher education
description: The study is a meta-analysis defined as "a strategic and scientific analysis of individual research conducted by other researchers." Data were collected from two library search engines (discovery search and roadrunner search discovery service) and Google Scholar using keyword combinations such as 'Latinos and success and technology'. Six articles were found; two were deleted because data came from an institution other than higher education, leaving four articles published between 2001 and 2014 for analysis.
requirements: Searches limited to two keywords across three search engines due to limited time and money
constraints: One applicable article was not used due to limited funds; one search result was in a foreign language; two articles were excluded for focusing on K-12 instead of higher education
target_learners: Latino-ethnic students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Identifying variables influencing academic success with technology
examples: The goal to attain between four to ten articles was met, with four articles analyzed

article_title: Determining the Effects of Reflection Type and Cognitive Style on Students' Content Knowledge
citation: Blackburn, J. J., Robinson, J. S., & Kacal, A. (2015). Determining the effects of reflection type and cognitive style on students' content knowledge. Journal of Agricultural Education, 56(3), 195-209. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2015.03195
title: Lab-Aids Biofuels: Investigating Ethanol Production and Combustion classroom kit (Investigation 2)
description: The agriscience laboratory experiment employed a kit designed by Lab-Aids titled Biofuels: Investigating Ethanol Production and Combustion. Specifically, students completed investigation two, titled Comparing the Energy Stored in Two Fuels, in which they compared the energy levels of ethanol and kerosene. Students formulated hypotheses, completed the experimental investigation, and employed mathematical formulae and calculations for testing their hypotheses. Major concepts included the chemical make-up of fuels, pollutants, experimental design and control, converting units of measurement, and averaging.
requirements: Students were provided laboratory protocols based on the Lab-Aids investigation to ensure fidelity of the treatment
constraints: The study used only investigation two of the kit, comparing energy levels of two fuels (ethanol and kerosene)
target_learners: undergraduate preservice agriculture teachers
target_learning_goals: scientific problem solving and experimental design
examples: The 25-item criterion-referenced test was developed based on content and questions found in the Lab-Aids curriculum booklet of scripted laboratory exercises

article_title: Comparison of Movement Notation (Laban) and Traditional Methodological Learning Success in Teaching Folk Dances
citation: Dilek Cantekin Elyağutu and Muhsin Hazar. (2017). Comparison of movement notation (Laban) and traditional methodological learning success in teaching folk dances. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.3118
title: Labanotation as a cognitive, notation-based teaching method for folk dance
description: The article presents Laban movement notation, created in 1928 by Rudolf Van Laban, as "a writing system in which all movements that can be made by the body are simply taken into account". Its vertical staff represents the human body from the dancer's point of view. The authors argue it grounds dance teaching in cognitive bases, supporting coding, analysis and synthesis, and serves as a record analogous to music notation for dance.
requirements: Learners must first be taught the symbol system; the study spent the first 7 weeks introducing symbols, reading, dictation and deciphering of motifs
constraints: The authors note the notation takes a long time to learn
target_learners: conservatory students in Turkish Folk Dance departments
examples: In the study, Laban group students learned Harmandalı dance motifs via notation symbols, dictation and deciphering over 14 weeks

article_title: The Effects of L1 and L2 Group Discussions on L2 Reading Comprehension
citation: Turnbull, B., & Sweetnam Evans, M. (2017). The effects of L1 and L2 group discussions on L2 reading comprehension. Reading in a Foreign Language, 29(1), 133–154. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl
title: Languaging within sociocultural theory as a framework for L1 group discussion and L2 reading comprehension
description: The article draws on Vygotsky's sociocultural theory and Swain's (2006) notion of languaging, defined as "the process of making meaning and shaping knowledge and experience through language" which "serves to mediate cognition". Speaking in the L1 is held to let learners engage in higher levels of cognitive activity than languaging in a less competent L2. The framework explains why L1 discussion groups scaffolded one another and accessed L1 reading strategies.
requirements: Discussion opportunities that allow learners to verbalise thoughts in their L1
constraints: The article grounds the framework in a small study of intermediate-level Japanese learners of English
target_learners: Japanese university students of intermediate-level English
key_sources: Turnbull, B., & Sweetnam Evans, M. (2017). The effects of L1 and L2 group discussions on L2 reading comprehension. Reading in a Foreign Language, 29(1), 133–154. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl

article_title: A laddered training model for breast surgery specialists: development and validation of a CBME-based precision education framework.
citation: Xu Kailun, Jiang Lingting, Zhang Yun, Du Yushen, Shen Yong, Chen Yiding, Shao Yingkuan. (2026). A laddered training model for breast surgery specialists: development and validation of a CBME-based precision education framework. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09688-5
title: A three-tiered laddered CBME training model for breast surgery: L1 basic skills, L2 minor procedures, L3 advanced surgery
description: The article introduces a stepwise, competency-based training model that categorizes breast surgery training into three sequential levels: L1 basic skills (ultrasound-guided biopsy, 1 month), L2 minor procedures (venous access port implantation, 2 months), and L3 advanced surgery (breast-conserving surgery, 3 months). Progression to each subsequent level requires completion of predefined objectives and competency requirements of the preceding stage. The model reorganizes case-driven clinical exposure into sequential, competency-based practice without extending the 6-month rotation period. Ultrasound serves as a bridging technology across all three tiers.
requirements: Completion of predefined objectives and competency requirements of the preceding stage before progression
A fixed 6-month rotation period within which training time is redistributed rather than expanded
Ultrasound as a bridging technology across diagnostic and procedural milestones
constraints: Implemented within a single tertiary hospital setting
A 6-month training period inadequate for longitudinal competency assessment
Absence of individualized adaptation strategies for residents with varying baseline abilities
target_learners: Second- and third-year breast surgery residents in standardized training
examples: Residents were preferentially matched with L1-level procedures as new trainees, with progression to L2- or L3-level procedures gated on completing prior-stage competency requirements
key_sources: Xu Kailun, Jiang Lingting, Zhang Yun, Du Yushen, Shen Yong, Chen Yiding, Shao Yingkuan. (2026). A laddered training model for breast surgery specialists: development and validation of a CBME-based precision education framework. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09688-5

article_title: Data driven student support: utilize the LASSI to improve academic performance.
citation: Zhou Yuanyuan, Sechelski Amber, Mowdy Brent, Johnson Tess, Vernardo Nikea, West Courtney A. (2026). Data driven student support: utilize the LASSI to improve academic performance. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09519-7
title: Use LASSI data proactively to design targeted academic support rather than remediation
description: The article recommends using the LASSI as a formative tool to inform proactive programmatic planning for academic support. Rather than "relying primarily on remediation after academic difficulty occurs, practitioners can use early LASSI data to inform targeted workshops, individualized coaching, and course-embedded instruction". The authors emphasize interpretation by learning specialists at individual and cohort levels, with aggregated profiles guiding adaptive support programming.

title: LapSim laparoscopic simulator with GOALS-aligned metrics and a structured SBT program (1-hour orientation plus 4-hour simulator session with individualized instructor feedback)
description: The LapSim (Surgical Science Ltd, Gothenburg, Sweden) laparoscopic simulator provides automated performance metrics grouped according to the Global Operative Assessment of Laparoscopic Skills (GOALS) rating scale. title: Structured feedback and video debriefing intervention with LabelMe CVS and Go/No-Go zone annotation
description: A post-procedure feedback intervention in which a trained tutor and trainee jointly review video of the performed laparoscopic cholecystectomy, "reflecting on important steps, complications, and potential improvement of the performance of the procedure". Video debriefing annotates four predefined video frames on the open-source platform LabelMe: instrument insertion, first cauterization, identification of the cystic duct and artery, and 10 s before clipping. Tutor and trainee annotate safe (Go) and dangerous (No-Go) zones of dissection in the first two frames and the CVS structures in frames 3 and 4.
requirements: A trained tutor to conduct the joint video debriefing and annotation after each procedure
Video capture of each ex-vivo porcine LC and the open-source annotation tool LabelMe
constraints: The study could not discern the impact of structured feedback, video debriefing, and annotation individually, as the intervention contained three potentially independent factors

target_learning_goals: achievement of the critical view of safety
examples: After each of four ex-vivo porcine LCs, feedback-group trainees received the joint video assessment and annotated Go/No-Go zones and CVS structures with the tutor using LabelMe

article_title: Undergraduate Lay Theories of Abilities: Mindset, universality, and brilliance beliefs uniquely predict undergraduate educational outcomes.
citation: Limeri Lisa B., Carter Nathan T., Lyra Franchesca, Martin Joel, Mastronardo Halle, Patel Jay, Dolan Erin L. (2023). Undergraduate Lay Theories of Abilities: Mindset, universality, and brilliance beliefs uniquely predict undergraduate educational outcomes. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.22-12-0250
title: Lay theories of abilities framework: mindset, universality, and brilliance as three distinct belief systems
description: This framework organizes students' beliefs about their cognitive abilities into three lay theories. As the article defines them, "Mindset refers to beliefs about the extent to which intelligence is improvable or innate," "Universality refers to beliefs about who (i.e., everyone, or only some people) has the potential for excellence," and "Brilliance refers to beliefs about whether success in a field requires raw intellectual talent." The framework holds that these beliefs act as meaning systems shaping how students interpret academic cues, set goals, respond to failure, experience belonging, and persist. Universality further divides into universal and nonuniversal beliefs, and mindset into growth and fixed dimensions, giving five first-order factors under two second-order factors.
requirements: Measurement requires context-appropriate instruments; the article argues high-quality measures were needed because existing scales were proof-of-concept tools or used the unreliably interpreted term intelligence
constraints: The three theories were historically studied in isolation, and the article notes it remained unclear whether brilliance is distinct from universality prior to this work
Mindset intervention success has been variable, which the article says suggests further research is necessary
target_learners: Undergraduate students in science and math fields
target_learning_goals: Understanding how beliefs about ability relate to motivation, belonging, goal orientation, self-handicapping, persistence, and achievement
examples: The article's phase-4 hypothesized-relationships table maps each lay theory dimension to predicted directions with belonging, evaluative concern, goal orientations, self-handicapping, persistence intent, and course grades

title: Novel unvalidated laparoscopic transfer task combining FLS cutting and suturing skills
description: The authors developed a 40-minute transfer task in which participants cut a three-dimensional red-marked shape from an upright foam piece along two 1 mm lines while moving the foam with a grasper, then sewed the remaining pieces together with three single sutures. It combines the skills of the three FLS tasks, allows camera adjustment as in real surgery, and is scored by time, miscuts, and knot/suture correctness. The authors created it because some authors call for more complex and clinically relevant exercises.

Scoring analogous to the FLS task sub-steps

It was combined with common FLS tasks for this reason

title: Lap-PASS LP-100: a VR simulator with haptic feedback that trains tissue traction for laparoscopic sigmoid colectomy dissection

title: Domain-specificity of psychomotor skills: laparoscopy and robotic surgery as different skill domains
description: The article proposes that laparoscopy and robot-assisted surgery may constitute distinct skill domains with limited overlap. The authors state, "In our view, laparoscopy and robotic surgery are different domains, perhaps requiring different skills," and note the Senhance uses non-wristed instruments that mimic laparoscopy, making it a robot-assisted digital laparoscopy device. This account explains the absence of transfer from laparoscopy training to robotic task performance.
requirements: Skills transfer between domains should not be assumed; training should target the target domain's own devices and tasks
constraints: Findings apply to limited laparoscopy exposure (0–40 min) and basic manipulation tasks on the Senhance system; transfer effects may be more pronounced with difficult tasks such as suturing, per cited studies
target_learners: novice medical students and surgical trainees
target_learning_goals: psychomotor skill acquisition for minimally invasive surgery
examples: The study's null result across all objective measures is the article's evidence for this domain-specificity account

title: Law et al.'s seven-factor model of intrinsic and extrinsic learning motivating factors
description: The study adopts the Learning Motivating Factors model of Law et al., which combines intrinsic and extrinsic motivation factors: "(1) an individual attitude and expectation factor", "(2) a challenging goals factor", "(3) a clear direction factor", "(4) a reward and recognition factor", "(5) a punishment factor", "(6) a social pressure and competition factor", and "(7) an efficacy factor". Intrinsic motivation encompasses individual attitude and expectation and challenging goals, whereas extrinsic motivation includes clear direction, reward and recognition, punishment, social pressure, and competition. The article operationalizes these with the 19-item Learning Motivating Factors Questionnaire on a 6-point Likert scale.
requirements: Measured with the Learning Motivating Factors Questionnaire subscales; the article reports internal consistency α of the instrument was 0.95 in prior research
constraints: The article notes computer learners' learning motivating factors are under-researched and some prior findings are confusing
target_learners: e-learners in computer programming courses
university students studying remotely
examples: The study applied the questionnaire alongside the PHQ-9, GAD-7, and MFI-20 to 444 e-learners and used the subscales as predictors in ANOVA, regression, and SEM models
